tool.name: ArcChordRatio
tool.summary: Computes the Arc-Chord Ratio (ACR) rugosity index (Du Preez 2015): a surface-roughness measure decoupled from slope. Each cell's three-dimensional surface area is divided by the area of its plane of best fit (rather than its flat footprint), so a smooth tilted surface scores 1 and only genuine roughness raises the value. An optional local-detrending step (Dilts et al. 2023) maps fine-scale roughness (ACR-L). Correct on geographic (latitude/longitude) DEMs.
tool.usage:
Rugosity - the ratio of a surface's true (contoured) area to a planar reference area - is one of the most widely used measures of terrain and seabed structural complexity. The traditional "surface ratio" (Jenness 2004; see the Surface Area and Ratio tool) uses the horizontal cell footprint as that reference, which ties the index to slope: a perfectly smooth but steeply tilted surface has a surface ratio well above 1, so slope and roughness are confounded. Du Preez (2015) resolves this with the Arc-Chord Ratio (ACR): the surface is instead projected onto its plane of best fit (the "chord" beneath the rugged "arc") before the planar area is measured. Because the reference plane tilts with the surface, a smooth tilted plane has ACR = 1 (the minimum) regardless of its slope, and values above 1 reflect genuine surface roughness rather than steepness.
For a raster, ACR is computed per cell over its 3 x 3 neighborhood, following Du Preez's own steps for the elevation-raster case: the contoured area is the three-dimensional surface area from the 8-triangle method of Jenness (2004); the plane of best fit is the standard 3 x 3 (Horn) surface, and its planar area is the horizontal cell area divided by the cosine of that plane's slope. Dividing contoured area by this tilted planar area is algebraically identical to taking the ordinary Jenness surface ratio and multiplying it by the cosine of the best-fit-plane slope - so ACR is simply the surface ratio "de-tilted", removing the slope inflation. ACR values start at 1 for flat or smoothly sloped terrain and rise with roughness.
Where ACR fits among ruggedness indices. Dilts et al. (2023) group ruggedness measures into three "generations". First-generation indices measure elevation variability and remain correlated with slope - the surface ratio (Jenness 2004), the Terrain Ruggedness Index (Riley 1999), and the Land Surface Ruggedness Index (Beasom 1983) belong here. Second-generation indices measure aspect diversity and remove the slope correlation - the Vector Ruggedness Measure (Sappington et al. 2007) and this Arc-Chord Ratio (Du Preez 2015). Both first- and second-generation indices, however, are still inflated by smooth folds: ridgelines and drainages read as rugged simply because adjacent cells face different directions, even where the surface is smooth. The third generation removes that too, by locally detrending the DEM first (see below).
Optional local detrending (Dilts et al. 2023). Turning on "Remove smooth topography first" subtracts a circular neighborhood mean of the DEM (the smoothing radius you set, default 1.5 cells = a 3 x 3 mean) before ACR is computed, leaving only the fine-scale surface variation. The result is Dilts's "local" variant (ACR-L), a third-generation index that isolates surface roughness itself: it passes all three of their "ideal ruggedness" criteria - independent of slope, unaffected by smooth folding, and rising only with true vertical roughness. Because ACR is inherently a 3 x 3 measure, the detrending window is the tool's scale control: a larger smoothing radius removes broader-scale topography before the roughness is measured.
Unlike a planar calculation, this tool is accurate for DEMs in geographic coordinate systems: both the surface area and the best-fit-plane slope are computed from true spheroidal distances at every row's latitude. Elevation units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when one is defined (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters); otherwise the tool asks you to choose meters or feet. Corner elevations for the surface-area step use either the original diagonal-midpoint interpolation or the more accurate 4-cell corner average (identical on planar slopes). ACR is NoData wherever any cell of the 3 x 3 neighborhood is NoData and on the raster's outer edge. The output is floating point and carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling. This tool reads the whole DEM into memory at once.
References: Du Preez, C. 2015. A new arc-chord ratio (ACR) rugosity index for quantifying three-dimensional landscape structural complexity. Landscape Ecology 30:181-192 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-014-0118-8). Surface area method: Jenness, J. S. 2004. Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839. Best-fit-plane slope from Horn's gradient: Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47. Ruggedness "generations" framework and the optional local detrending: Dilts, T. E., M. E. Blum, K. T. Shoemaker, P. J. Weisberg, and K. M. Stewart. 2023. Improved topographic ruggedness indices more accurately model fine-scale ecological patterns. Landscape Ecology 38:1395-1410 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-023-01646-6).

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute ACR from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.

The output ACR rugosity raster (floating point; 1 on flat or smoothly sloped terrain, higher where the surface is rough; NoData on the raster edge and wherever any cell of the 3 x 3 neighborhood is NoData). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.

How the elevation at each corner of the cell is interpolated for the surface-area step. Diagonal midpoint (2 cells, original method) averages the focal and diagonal cell centers, matching the legacy DEM Surface Tools. Corner average (4 cells) averages all four cells sharing the corner - the true bilinear estimate at that point. The two methods are identical on a planar slope and differ only where the surface curves.

Turn on to locally detrend the DEM before computing ACR (Dilts et al. 2023): a circular neighborhood mean is subtracted from the DEM, leaving only the fine-scale surface variation, so smooth ridgelines and drainages no longer read as rugged. The result is Dilts's local variant, ACR-L. Off by default (the standard ACR).

The radius of the circular neighborhood mean used to smooth the DEM for detrending. The default, 1.5 cells, is exactly a 3 x 3 mean (the smoothing Dilts et al. 2023 used); larger radii remove broader-scale topography before the roughness is measured. Only used when Remove smooth topography first is on.

Units for the smoothing (detrending) radius: Cells, or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles) converted to cells from the cell size - planarly for projected rasters, geodesically per row for geographic rasters. Only used when detrending is on.

scriptExample.title: Arc-Chord Ratio example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Standard ACR, then the local (detrended) variant ACR-L with a 3x3 smoothing window. Valid corner_method values: "Diagonal midpoint (2 cells, original method)", "Corner average (4 cells)". Valid detrend_units: "Cells", "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles".
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.ArcChordRatio( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_ACR", elev_units="Meters", corner_method="Corner average (4 cells)") arcpy.jenness.ArcChordRatio( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_ACRL", elev_units="Meters", corner_method="Corner average (4 cells)", detrend=True, detrend_radius=1.5, detrend_units="Cells")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Arc-Chord Ratio (ACR) rugosity: surface roughness decoupled from slope (Du Preez 2015) - a cell's 3-D surface area divided by the area of its plane of best fit, equivalently the Jenness (2004) surface ratio times the cosine of the 3x3 best-fit-plane slope - with an optional local-detrending step (Dilts et al. 2023) and correct geodesic handling of geographic DEMs.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes the Arc-Chord Ratio (ACR) rugosity index from a single-band DEM (Du Preez 2015). For each cell, the three-dimensional surface area (8-triangle method, Jenness 2004) is divided by the area of the surface projected onto its 3x3 plane of best fit; equivalently, ACR is the Jenness surface ratio multiplied by the cosine of the best-fit-plane (Horn) slope. Because the reference plane tilts with the surface, ACR is decoupled from slope: a smooth tilted plane has ACR = 1 (the minimum) and larger values indicate genuine surface roughness. Optionally the DEM is locally detrended first (subtracting a circular neighborhood mean; Dilts et al. 2023) to map fine-scale roughness (ACR-L), a third-generation ruggedness index. Distances and the best-fit-plane slope are computed per row on the spheroid for geographic DEMs. The output is floating point and carries statistics and a histogram. References: Du Preez, C. 2015. Landscape Ecology 30:181-192; Jenness, J. S. 2004. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839; Dilts, T. E., et al. 2023. Landscape Ecology 38:1395-1410.
